newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia police ban gatherings in Central Java.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia police ban gatherings in Central Java.

text.p: Police have banned mass gatherings in four towns in Indonesia's Central Java province after a series of clashes between supporters of rival political parties, the official Antara news agency reported on Saturday.
The news agency quoted a senior police officer as saying no gatherings would be allowed in the four towns ahead of the start of the campaign for May 29 general elections.

"I have already instructed all police chiefs in Temanggung, Wonosobo, Kebumen and Magelang towns not to issue permits for such activities," Colonel Apit Endang Rustandi was quoted as saying by Antara.
Antara gave no further details. The official campaign will start on April 27.

At least three government offices, 11 vehicles and dozens of homes were damaged and 14 people were injured in Wonosobo in clashes between supporters of the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the ruling Golkar party on Wednesday, newspapers said.
On the same day, a group of PPP supporters clashed with police near the neighbouring town of Banjarnegara after they damaged a number of buildings and robbed fruit vendors.

Wonosobo police chief Colonel Binarto said five people had been questioned after the riot in the town, 350 km (215 miles) southeast of Jakarta, and two of had been formally charged. Antara give no further details.
Several towns in Central Java have been rocked by violence in the past two weeks, with recurring clashes between supporters of the PPP and Golkar.

Riots broke out in the coastal town of Pekalongan, a PPP stronghold, two weeks ago after reports that a popular folk singer who has campaigned for the PPP in the past would be a Golkar candidate in the elections.

Central Java military commander Major-General Soebagyo, commenting on the riots, urged the public on Friday not to be easily provoked by people who wanted to disrupt next month's general elections, Antara reported.
Only three political parties -- the PPP, Golkar and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- are allowed to contest the elections.
In the last parliamentary elections in 1992, Golkar won 68 percent of the vote, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
Golkar is certain to win this year's polls, but party leaders have said they want to increase their vote to above 70 percent.
